A large clinical trial has found that a community-based prevention strategy reduced new HIV infections by 70 percent in participating rural districts compared with control districts. The strategy combined routine testing, same-day treatment initiation, and outreach by trained local health workers. Over three years, investigators enrolled more than 40,000 adults across 48 districts. The reduction held across age groups and was similar for men and women. “These results show what is possible when services are brought close to where people live,” said the principal investigator. The research team is now working with health ministries to assess costs and plan for wider rollout. The study was supported by the institute and conducted in collaboration with local partners, and results will be presented at an upcoming international conference.
